Regular vs "uncensored" Qwen3.8-27B on a Mac Studio

 I ran both 4-bit MLX variants of Qwen3.8-27B through my full deployment benchmark on an M4 Max 128GB: 76 scenarios × 2 repeats, thinking off, no output caps, native MTP speculative decoding, One is the standard mlx-community conversion; the other is abliterated from @OrcaRouter 

 Headline: 89.9 vs 89.8 TrueScore. A tie.

 But the domains tell the real story:

 Where abliteration hurt
 • Safety: 65.4 vs 80.3
 • Robustness (knowing when to abstain): 75.5 vs 100
 • Code: 91.1 vs 96.6
 • Pass@1: 90.8% vs 94.7%

 Where the abliterated model won
 • Agentic multi-tool work: 98.9 vs 91.6
 • Visual/canvas generation: 90.6 vs 77.6
 • Tool use: 82.9 vs 78.4

 Identical on both: planning, structured output, composition (all 100), and the honest negative, long-context retrieval at just 55.9. That weakness is the base model's, and neither quantization nor surgery touched it.

 My read: abliteration isn't a free lunch and isn't a lobotomy. It traded refusal behavior and some caution for measurably more aggressive task completion. Pick by workload.

 Disclosures: the two use different spec-decode drafters (BF16 vs 4-bit MTP), so this is a deployment-level comparison, not an isolated abliteration study. Serial requests on a live desktop — no throughput claims. Zero transport errors both runs, zero repeat flakiness (deterministic at temp 0.3).

Fable 5.1 same prompt for the ship in a bottle

Ocean is 4,080 instanced voxel columns. Height = swell (4 travelling wave components) + a ripple field solved each frame with the 2D wave equation, damping, and reflection off the glass and the island.

The ripple field is advected downstream at the ship’s sailing speed, so the bow disturbance spreads into a V-shaped wake behind the hull, with churned foam trailing off the stern.

Foam appears where wave fronts get steep (breaking crests) and where ripples are energetic.

The galleon floats by sampling water height at bow, stern, port and starboard, then driving heave, pitch and roll through spring–damper dynamics — so it lags, overshoots and settles like a real hull. When the bow slams down faster than the water is falling, it throws spray particles and kicks a ripple.

Waves wash up the beach because columns only exist where the surface is above the sand.

GLM-5.3 Flash quant showdown on 2× DGX Spark per model.

Bench v6.7.1 — 76 scenarios × 2 repeats.

EXL3 TR3 4bpw
• TrueScore: 90.9
• Capability: 92.2
• Operational: 87.6
• Median turn: 4.30s
• Long-response effective rate: ~35.4 tok/s
• 53,347 total output tokens

NVFP4
• Raw TrueScore: 78.5
• Capability: 71.6
• Operational: 71.9
• Median turn: 13.42s
• Long-response effective rate: ~26.5 tok/s
• 996,608 total output tokens

EXL3 won instruction following (94.2 vs 48.9), structured output (97.2 vs 12.8), code (98.1 vs 68.5), visuals (92.3 vs 36.3), long context (100 vs 85.3) and robustness (100 vs 86.8).

NVFP4 won agentic work (98.5 vs 88.0), planning (100 vs 91.2) and narrowly won safety (87.8 vs 85.6). Tool use tied at 78.4.

NVFP4 completed every request with zero transport errors, but emitted 18.7× more output and took 3.12× longer per median turn.

Important: this is a deployment comparison, not a pure quant-only test. EXL3 used FP8 KV, CUDA graphs and a configured 1M context ceiling. NVFP4 used Marlin, FP8 E4M3 KV, eager mode and a 262K ceiling.

Verdict: EXL3 TR3 4bpw was the much better all-around deployment. NVFP4 was genuinely strong for planning and agentic workflows, but its verbosity and format behavior need fixing before it can compete on practical quality and speed.

Two updates on the Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 + DFlash2 Spark recipe, both of which humbled me a bit.

1. The new official NVFP4 checkpoint with BF16 lm_head dropped and I assumed it would be a free quality win. Wrong. It's 40% slower (42 to 25 tok/s) because the DFlash2 draft was tuned against the quantized head's logits. Swap the head, acceptance falls from 4.8 to 3.2. And quality didn't move at all, 66-67/80 GSM8K either way. The quantized head + FP32 ranking workaround from r0b0tlab beats the clean fix. Lesson: spec decode couples the draft to your target's exact numerics. I compared before testing all sides of it.

2. r0b0tlab also pointed out our published numbers undersell the recipe since random token benching is the drafter's worst case. He's right. Real code prompts hit accept lengths of 9.6-10 out of a max 10, pushing C1 from 42 to as high as 66 tok/s. Even 96K context tasks hold 41-47 tok/s. So 42 is the floor, not the ceiling.

Full data going in the repo.

how our code bench works (sparkbench challenge):
• 3 hard coding tasks in the challenge set (CODE-12 / 13 / 14)
• model has to emit real python
• we execute it in a sandbox against unit tests
• score is tests passed, not vibes or “looks clean”
• think off, temp 0.3, 3 repeats so flaky wins don’t stick

so “best at code” here means best at single-shot executable problems under that contract.
not “best agent that can ship a whole feature over 40 tool calls.”
